claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim presented in the abstract without direct empirical support in this statement.

claims.claim: The degree of interhemispheric rs-FC within fronto-temporal auditory networks predicts learning, transmission, and structural modification of an artificial tone system weeks after scanning.
claims.source: We found that the degree of interhemispheric rs-FC within fronto-temporal auditory networks predicts—weeks after scanning—learning, transmission, and structural modification of an artificial tone system.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from fMRI and behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Human brain function shows substantial variability across individuals.
claims.source: Human brain function shows substantial variability across individuals (Bergfeldt, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bergfeldt, 2016.

claims.claim: Symbolic systems including language and music evolve while being transmitted across individuals and generations, partly adapting to properties of brain systems of learners and users.
claims.source: In recent years, it has been argued that symbolic systems, including language and music, evolve while they are being transmitted across individuals and generations, partly adapting to properties of brain systems of learners and users (Deacon, 1997; Christiansen and Chater, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deacon, 1997 and Christiansen and Chater, 2008.

claims.claim: Laboratory experiments have shown that novel and initially unstructured artificial signaling systems become gradually more organized during transmission along chains of individuals.
claims.source: These studies showed that novel and initially unstructured (artificial) signaling systems become gradually more organized during transmission along chains of individuals ('generations').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by references to laboratory experiments on cultural transmission.

claims.claim: Rs-FC is a measure of the temporal correlation of spontaneous slow fluctuations (<0.1 Hz) in the BOLD signal between spatially separated brain regions.
claims.source: Rs-FC is a measure of the temporal correlation of spontaneous slow fluctuations (<0.1 Hz) in the BOLD signal between spatially separated brain regions, derived from resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) data (Biswal, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to Biswal, 2012.

claims.claim: Rs-FC captures spontaneous interactions between neuronal populations in functionally associated networks.
claims.source: This measure is receiving much attention because it captures spontaneous interactions between neuronal populations in functionally associated networks (Damoiseaux et al., 2006), and it has been recognized as a promising tool for assessing individual differences in brain function (Dubois and Adolphs, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Damoiseaux et al., 2006 and Dubois and Adolphs, 2016.

claims.claim: Some musical traits and behaviors may be traced back to the local functioning of the auditory cortex.
claims.source: One hypothesis in the field of bio-musicology is that some musical traits and behaviors may be traced back to the local functioning of the auditory cortex (Trainor, 2015; Lumaca et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to Trainor, 2015 and Lumaca et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: Music material has to pass through an information processing 'bottleneck' that constrains music perception and acquisition with each generational transfer.
claims.source: With each generational transfer, music material has to pass through an information processing 'bottleneck' that constrains music perception and acquisition (Merker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Merker et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The information processing bottleneck can be instantiated in anatomical and functional connectivity patterns of the auditory system and other brain systems.
claims.source: Recent evidence indicates that this bottleneck can be instantiated in anatomical and functional connectivity patterns of the auditory system and other (e.g. attentional and motor) brain systems (Zatorre, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zatorre, 2013.

claims.claim: Stronger functional connectivity between left and right auditory cortex, and between auditory cortex and prefrontal areas during active listening, is associated with facilitation in the encoding and discrimination of melodic material.
claims.source: For example, a stronger functional connectivity between left and right auditory cortex, and between auditory cortex and prefrontal areas, as measured during active listening, tends to be associated with facilitation in the encoding and discrimination of melodic material in experimental participants (Andoh and Zatorre, 2011; Andoh and Zatorre, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andoh and Zatorre, 2011 and Andoh and Zatorre, 2013.

claims.claim: Functional connectivity networks measured at rest may serve as indicators of auditory learning skills.
claims.source: When measured at rest, functional connectivity networks may serve as indicators of auditory learning skills (Ventura-Campos et al., 2013; Veroude et al., 2010) and have been shown to be plastic and music-experience dependent (Fauvel et al., 2014; Tanaka and Kirino, 2016; Zamorano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Resting-state functional connectivity networks have been shown to be plastic and music-experience dependent.
claims.source: When measured at rest, functional connectivity networks may serve as indicators of auditory learning skills (Ventura-Campos et al., 2013; Veroude et al., 2010) and have been shown to be plastic and music-experience dependent (Fauvel et al., 2014; Tanaka and Kirino, 2016; Zamorano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fauvel et al., 2014; Tanaka and Kirino, 2016; Zamorano et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Individual players' ability to learn and transmit an artificial tone system in signaling games, and the extent to which structural aspects of the codes are reorganized, can be predicted based on the latency of the mismatch negativity (MMN).
claims.source: In previous work (Lumaca and Baggio, 2016), we showed that individual players' ability to learn and transmit an artificial tone system in signaling games, and the extent to which structural aspects of the codes are reorganized by players, can be predicted based on the latency of a neurophysiological marker of auditory processing in participants: the mismatch negativity (MMN) (Näätänen et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Lumaca and Baggio, 2016) and the definition of MMN from Näätänen et al., 1978.

claims.claim: Complex cultural phenomena such as the transmission of musical systems may be partly constrained by the functional organization of the auditory cortex in the human brain.
claims.source: Complex cultural phenomena, such as the transmission of musical systems (Le Bomin et al., 2016), may therefore be partly constrained by the functional organization of the auditory cortex in the human brain.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim inferred from previous findings, with a citation to Le Bomin et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Fifty-two right-handed volunteers with normal hearing participated in the study.
claims.source: Fifty-two right-handed volunteers (33 females, mean age 24.5 years, range 20–34) with normal hearing participated in the study (two additional participants did not go through the entire experimental MRI session since they experienced discomfort).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claims.claim: Fifty-one participants completed the entire experiment.
claims.source: Fifty-one of them completed the entire experiment: one person (female) dropped out before the behavioral part, due to reasons unrelated to the study.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the final study sample.

claims.claim: All participants were musically naive individuals with less than three years of formal musical training.
claims.source: Participants were all musically naive individuals (i.e., none of them had three or more years of formal musical training; mean 0.6 years ± 0.98).
claims.evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claims.claim: The two sessions occurred on average 20 days apart.
claims.source: Each participant took part in two sessions occurring on two separate days (mean 20 days apart, range 13–30 days).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design timing.

claims.claim: The Bohlen-Pierce scale was used to construct tone sequences in the oddball task and behavioral experiment.
claims.source: The tone sequences used in the oddball task and in the behavioral experiment were built using pure tones from the Bohlen-Pierce (BP) scale (Mathews et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used, with a citation to Mathews et al., 1988.

claims.claim: In the equal-tempered version of the BP scale, a tritave (3:1 frequency ratio) is divided into 13 logarithmically even steps.
claims.source: In the equal-tempered version of the BP scale, a tritave (3:1 frequency ratio) is divided into 13 logarithmically even steps, and the frequency (F) of each tone is given by the formula F = k X 3 (n/13), where n is the number of steps, and k is the fundamental frequency (see below).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the BP scale properties.

claims.claim: Standard sequences comprised 80% of trials in the oddball task.
claims.source: In a single run, participants were presented with repeated Standard sequences (80% of the trials), interspersed with Contour (10%) and Interval deviant sequences, adding up to 1260 stimuli.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the oddball task.

claims.claim: Contour deviant sequences comprised 10% of trials in the oddball task.
claims.source: In a single run, participants were presented with repeated Standard sequences (80% of the trials), interspersed with Contour (10%) and Interval deviant sequences, adding up to 1260 stimuli.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the oddball task.

claims.claim: Interval deviant sequences comprised 10% of trials in the oddball task.
claims.source: In a single run, participants were presented with repeated Standard sequences (80% of the trials), interspersed with Contour (10%) and Interval deviant sequences, adding up to 1260 stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the percentages given (80% + 10% + 10% = 100%).

claims.claim: In contour deviants, the fourth tone violated the surface structure of a sequence but not the interval size.
claims.source: In contour deviants, the fourth tone violated the surface structure ('ups' and 'downs') of a sequence, but not the interval size; vice versa for the interval deviants.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus design.

claims.claim: In interval deviants, the fourth tone violated the interval size but not the surface structure of a sequence.
claims.source: In contour deviants, the fourth tone violated the surface structure ('ups' and 'downs') of a sequence, but not the interval size; vice versa for the interval deviants.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus design.

claims.claim: Two deviant sequences of the same type were always presented in close temporal succession to obtain a stronger oddball BOLD response.
claims.source: To obtain a stronger oddball BOLD response, two deviant sequences of the same type (contour or interval) were always presented in close temporal succession (range 2400–4800 ms).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the experimental design.

claims.claim: Whole-brain data were acquired on a 3T MRI scanner (Siemens Prisma).
claims.source: Whole-brain data were acquired on a 3T MRI scanner (Siemens Prisma).
claims.evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition method.

claims.claim: For the rs-fMRI, a total of 600 volumes were acquired over 10 min using fast T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI) multiband sequence.
claims.source: For the rs-fMRI (resting state), a total of 600 volumes were acquired over 10 min using fast T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI) multiband sequence (TR, 1000 ms; TE, 29.6 ms; voxel size, 2.5 mm3).
claims.evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: For the functional localizer task, a total of 1535 volumes were acquired over 25 min using the same multiband EPI sequence.
claims.source: For the functional localizer task, a total of 1535 volumes were acquired over 25 min using the same multiband EPI sequence (TR, 1000 ms; TE, 29.6 ms; voxel size, 2.5 mm3).
claims.evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: Pre-processing and statistical analyses of fMRI data were performed using SPM12 (r7487), implemented in Matlab R2016b.
claims.source: Pre-processing and statistical analyses of fMRI data were performed using SPM12 (r7487), implemented in Matlab R2016b (Mathworks), and included all 52 participants.
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis software used.

claims.claim: Four ROIs were generated as 5 mm spheres centered on peak voxels from the auditory functional localizer task.
claims.source: Different regions of interest (ROIs), or seeds, were constructed as 5 mm spheres centered on the peak voxels from the auditory functional localizer task. Following this procedure, four ROIs were generated, centered on the following MNI coordinates (x y z): [54 2 -4], [−52–14 4], [66 -16 4], [−66–22 6].
claims.evidence: This describes the ROI definition method.

claims.claim: Resting-state functional connectivity preprocessing and analysis were implemented using a standard pipeline in the SPM CONN toolbox.
claims.source: Resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) preprocessing and analysis were implemented by using a standard pipeline in the SPM CONN toolbox (Whitfield-Gabrieli and Nieto-Castanon, 2012).
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis method with a citation.

claims.claim: Data were band-pass filtered at 0.008–0.09 Hz to reduce the effects of low-frequency drifts and high-frequency noise.
claims.source: Data were band-pass filtered at 0.008–0.09 Hz to reduce the effects of low-frequency drifts and high-frequency noise.
claims.evidence: This describes a preprocessing step.

claims.claim: In signaling games, a sender and a receiver exchange signals over subsequent rounds with the aim of developing a 'common code'.
claims.source: In the version adopted here, signaling games are cooperative games of incomplete information (Lewis, 1969), where a sender and a receiver exchange signals without a prior agreement on pairings of signals to meanings: players should then agree, over multiple signaling rounds, on a 'common code' (i.e. a shared set of signals-meaning mappings).
claims.evidence: This describes the signaling game paradigm with a citation to Lewis, 1969.

claims.claim: The signals in the signaling games were five isochronous melodic patterns of 5 sinusoidal tones, with each tone drawn from the BP scale.
claims.source: The signals were five isochronous melodic patterns of 5 sinusoidal tones, with each tone drawn from the BP scale (k = 440 Hz; n = 0, 4, 6, 7, 10); the states were five emotions, simple (peace, joy, sadness) and compound (peace X joy; peace X sadness), shown as facial expressions of one actor (for more details, see Lumaca and Baggio, 2016; Lumaca and Baggio, 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the signaling games.

claims.claim: The states in the signaling games were five emotions shown as facial expressions.
claims.source: The signals were five isochronous melodic patterns of 5 sinusoidal tones, with each tone drawn from the BP scale (k = 440 Hz; n = 0, 4, 6, 7, 10); the states were five emotions, simple (peace, joy, sadness) and compound (peace X joy; peace X sadness), shown as facial expressions of one actor (for more details, see Lumaca and Baggio, 2016; Lumaca and Baggio, 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the signaling games.

claims.claim: Each participant played 70 trials in Game 1 and 30 trials in Game 2.
claims.source: Each participant played 70 trials in Game 1 and 30 trials in Game 2.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: Asymmetry in Game 1 was −1 by design because the confederates never adjusted their code to the one used by the participants.
claims.source: Asymmetry in Game 1 was −1 by design: following the experimenter's instructions, the confederates never adjusted their code to the one used by the participants (receivers).
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Asymmetry in Game 2 was negative and significantly different from zero (median −0.4, Z = −6.05, p<0.001).
claims.source: Asymmetry in Game two was negative and significantly different from zero (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median −0.4, n = 51, Z = −6.05, p<0.001): there was a tendency for participants (now senders) to maintain their code and for receivers to adjust more frequently their mappings during coordination than senders did.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a tendency for participants as senders to maintain their code and for receivers to adjust more frequently their mappings during coordination than senders did.
claims.source: Asymmetry in Game two was negative and significantly different from zero (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median −0.4, n = 51, Z = −6.05, p<0.001): there was a tendency for participants (now senders) to maintain their code and for receivers to adjust more frequently their mappings during coordination than senders did.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the asymmetry result.

claims.claim: Coordination in Game 1 was positive and significantly different from 0 using both tone distance (median 0.76) and contour distance (median 0.84, Z = 6.21, p<0.001).
claims.source: Coordination in Game one was positive and significantly different from 0 using both tone distance (median 0.76) and contour distance (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median 0.84, n = 51, Z = 6.21, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Transmission was positive and different from 0, with better accuracy observed using contour distance (median 0.65, Z = 6.22, p<0.001) than tone distance (median 0.36, Z = 6.21, p<0.001).
claims.source: Transmission was positive and different from 0, with better accuracy observed using contour distance (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median 0.65, n = 51, Z = 6.22, p<0.001) than tone distance (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median 0.36, n = 51, Z = 6.21, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The initial material was successfully learned and then transmitted by all participants.
claims.source: The initial material was successfully learned and then transmitted by all participants.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral results.

claims.claim: Innovation was positive and different from 0, and it was higher for tone distance (median 0.64, Z = 6.22, p<0.001) than for contour distance (median 0.64, Z = 6.16, p<0.001).
claims.source: Innovation was positive and different from 0, and it was higher for tone distance (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median 0.64, n = 51, Z = 6.22, p<0.001) than for contour distance (one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test: median 0.64, n = 51, Z = 6.16, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data. Note: the medians appear identical in the text, which may be a typo in the original manuscript.

claims.claim: In Game 2, melodic signals were made less entropic, especially in their melodic contour (mean change 0.07, Z = 4.42, p<0.001).
claims.source: In Game 2, melodic signals were made less entropic, especially in their melodic contour (Wilcoxon signed rank test: code regularization, median mean change 0.08, n = 51, Z = 1.60, p=0.1; contour regularization, mean change 0.07, n = 51, Z = 4.42, p<0.001) and were biased toward smaller intervals (mean ICR change 0.15, n = 51, Z = −3.92, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: In Game 2, melodic signals were biased toward smaller intervals (mean ICR change 0.15, Z = −3.92, p<0.001).
claims.source: In Game 2, melodic signals were made less entropic, especially in their melodic contour (Wilcoxon signed rank test: code regularization, median mean change 0.08, n = 51, Z = 1.60, p=0.1; contour regularization, mean change 0.07, n = 51, Z = 4.42, p<0.001) and were biased toward smaller intervals (mean ICR change 0.15, n = 51, Z = −3.92, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Whole-brain analysis for the contrast between deviant contour and standard stimuli revealed sharp activations (pFWE <0.001) in regions of the left and right superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: Whole-brain analysis conducted for the contrast between deviant contour and standard stimuli (DC >SS) revealed sharp activations (pFWE <0.001) in regions of the left and right superior temporal gyrus (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis.

claims.claim: The analysis revealed four distinct clusters of activation in the bilateral STG: two anterior clusters localized in Heschl's gyrus and two more posterior localized in the planum temporale.
claims.source: Specifically, the analysis revealed four distinct clusters of activation in the bilateral STG: two anterior clusters, localized in Heschl's gyrus (HG; cytoarchitectonic areas Te1 and Te1.2, in the left and right hemisphere, respectively), and two more posterior, localized in the planum temporale (PT; cytoarchitectonic area Te3) (Morosan et al., 2005) (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis, with reference to Figure 4 and citation to Morosan et al., 2005.

claims.claim: No significant activations were detected for the contrast between interval deviant and standard stimuli.
claims.source: Conversely, no significant activations were detected for the contrast between interval deviant and standard stimuli (I-deviant >SS).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis.

claims.claim: Individuals with stronger inter-hemispheric rs-FC between ROIs of lateral STG displayed better learning performance and less innovation.
claims.source: Individuals with stronger inter-hemispheric rs-FC between ROIs of lateral STG displayed better learning performance and less innovation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the correlation results.

claims.claim: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r = 0.41; p=0.002).
claims.source: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r = 0.41; p=0.002), accuracy (r = 0.36; p=0.007), and transmission (r = 0.41; p=0.002) and negatively correlated with innovation (r = -0.41; p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with accuracy (r = 0.36; p=0.007).
claims.source: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r = 0.41; p=0.002), accuracy (r = 0.36; p=0.007), and transmission (r = 0.41; p=0.002) and negatively correlated with innovation (r = -0.41; p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with transmission (r = 0.41; p=0.002).
claims.source: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r = 0.41; p=0.002), accuracy (r = 0.36; p=0.007), and transmission (r = 0.41; p=0.002) and negatively correlated with innovation (r = -0.41; p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Fisher's z values were negatively correlated with innovation (r = -0.41; p=0.003).
claims.source: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r = 0.41; p=0.002), accuracy (r = 0.36; p=0.007), and transmission (r = 0.41; p=0.002) and negatively correlated with innovation (r = -0.41; p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: A negative correlation was observed between innovation and rs-FC between left STG and left HG (r = −0.41; p=0.002).
claims.source: A negative correlation was also observed between innovation and rs-FC between left STG and left HG (r = −0.41; p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Fisher's z values were positively correlated with regularization of melodic contour (r = 0.43; p=0.001).
claims.source: Individuals with stronger connectivity tend to regularize the signals' melodic contour more (i.e. they tend to reduce contour entropy) (r = 0.43; p=0.001) and to introduce smaller intervals in signals compared to players with weaker rs-FC (this result did not survive Bonferroni correction; p=0.01) (see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for a correlation across all behavioral measures).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: FC between left HG ROI and a cluster including right middle and superior frontal gyri was negatively correlated with melodic regularization (r = −0.58; p<0.001).
claims.source: Figure 6 shows that FC between left HG ROI and a cluster including right middle and superior frontal gyri was negatively correlated with melodic regularization (r = −0.58; p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the whole-brain FC analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claims.claim: Individuals who reproduced smoother melodic material in Game 2 tended to have a stronger negative correlation between spontaneous activity in the left primary auditory cortex and right prefrontal regions.
claims.source: Individuals who reproduced smoother melodic material in Game 2 tended to have a stronger negative correlation between spontaneous activity in the left primary auditory cortex and right prefrontal regions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the FC result.

claims.claim: Digit span scores were not predictive of learning behavior and structural regularization in signaling games.
claims.source: As shown in Table 1, digit span scores were not predictive of learning behavior and structural regularization in signaling games (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: Percent signal change values obtained for each ROI did not predict behavior or structural changes in signaling games.
claims.source: Percent signal change values obtained for each ROI in the same contrast (DC >SS) did not predict behavior or structural changes in signaling games (all p-values>0.05 uncorrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the analysis of task-based activity.

claims.claim: Changes in task-dependent functional connectivity did not predict behavior or structural changes in signaling games.
claims.source: Changes in task-dependent functional connectivity did not predict behavior or structural changes in signaling games (no suprathreshold voxel were found; all p-values>0.05 uncorrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the PPI analysis.

claims.claim: Rs-FC between homologous portions of the left and right STG predicts individual behavior in learning, transmission, and reorganization of artificial tone systems.
claims.source: Using a large sample of participants (N = 51), we showed that rs-FC between homologous portions of the left and right STG predicts individual behavior in learning, transmission, and reorganization of artificial tone systems.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claims.claim: The structural reorganization of melodic patterns was only predicted by rs-FC between the left and right Heschl's gyri, and between left Heschl's gyrus and prefrontal regions.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the structural reorganization of melodic patterns was only predicted by rs-FC between the left and right Heschl's gyri, and between left Heschl's gyrus and prefrontal regions, while learning and transmission were only predicted by rs-FC between areas of bilateral planum temporale.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the dissociation found in the results.

claims.claim: Learning and transmission were only predicted by rs-FC between areas of bilateral planum temporale.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that the structural reorganization of melodic patterns was only predicted by rs-FC between the left and right Heschl's gyri, and between left Heschl's gyrus and prefrontal regions, while learning and transmission were only predicted by rs-FC between areas of bilateral planum temporale.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the dissociation found in the results.

claims.claim: This suggests a functional dissociation in the bilateral fronto-temporal auditory network for encoding and regularization of musical material.
claims.source: This suggests a functional dissociation in the bilateral fronto-temporal auditory network for encoding and regularization of musical material.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the dissociation found in the results.

claims.claim: Task-driven activations did not predict behavior in signaling games.
claims.source: Task-driven activations did not predict behavior in signaling games.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the null result for task-based activations.

claims.claim: The bilateral activation in the STG includes the main cortical generators of the auditory MMN.
claims.source: The bilateral activation in the STG, as evoked by deviant contour changes in an oddball functional localizer (Lumaca and Baggio, 2016), includes the main cortical generators of the auditory MMN (Opitz et al., 1999; Opitz et al., 2002; Wible et al., 2001; Schönwiesner et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on MMN generators.

claims.claim: The MMN reflects auditory change-detection and can be used to study bottom-up processes of auditory scene analysis.
claims.source: The MMN reflects auditory change-detection and can therefore be used to study bottom-up processes of auditory scene analysis (ASA), such as the extraction of regularities from acoustic inputs, and melodic and rhythmic grouping during encoding of melodic Gestalts (Bregman, 1990; Koelsch and Siebel, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bregman, 1990 and Koelsch and Siebel, 2005.

claims.claim: The absence of significant activations for deviant interval changes is consistent with previous findings suggesting that automatic detection in non-musicians is more difficult for pitch interval changes relative to contour changes.
claims.source: The absence of significant activations for deviant interval changes is consistent with previous findings suggesting that automatic detection (smaller and slower MMN) in non-musicians is more difficult for pitch interval changes relative to contour changes (Schiavetto et al., 1999; Trainor et al., 2002), here further hindered by the use of the unfamiliar Bohlen-Pierce scale (Leung and Dean, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schiavetto et al., 1999; Trainor et al., 2002; and Leung and Dean, 2018.

claims.claim: The results support the view that automatic detection of deviant sounds and pre-attentive operations of ASA are primarily carried out in early auditory cortices.
claims.source: Our results support the view that automatic detection of deviant sounds and, more generally, pre-attentive operations of ASA are primarily carried out in early auditory cortices (Schindler et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, supported by a citation to Schindler et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The 'neuronal recycling' hypothesis proposes that acquired cultural systems and behaviors are accommodated within pre-existing brain networks, initially evolved for different specific adaptive reasons.
claims.source: The 'neuronal recycling' hypothesis (Dehaene and Cohen, 2007) is a comprehensive view that may also account for the neural origins of cultural variation. Acquired cultural systems and behaviors are accommodated within pre-existing brain networks, initially evolved for different specific adaptive reasons.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the neuronal recycling hypothesis with a citation to Dehaene and Cohen, 2007.

claims.claim: Cultural systems and behaviors may be shaped by the computational constraints inherent to the host networks.
claims.source: Such systems and behaviors may then be shaped by the computational constraints inherent to the host networks.
claims.evidence: This is part of the neuronal recycling hypothesis.

claims.claim: Auditory scene analysis emerges early in human development.
claims.source: Auditory scene analysis (ASA) emerges early in human development (Winkler et al., 2003), and it is automatic and widely conserved across species (Fay, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Winkler et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Auditory scene analysis is automatic and widely conserved across species.
claims.source: Auditory scene analysis (ASA) emerges early in human development (Winkler et al., 2003), and it is automatic and widely conserved across species (Fay, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fay, 2008.

claims.claim: ASA neural circuitry might be evolutionarily older than human musicality and may provide some of the neuronal substrates for the cultural recycling of music.
claims.source: ASA neural circuitry might therefore be evolutionarily older than human musicality and may provide some of the neuronal substrates for the cultural recycling of music (Trainor, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Trainor, 2015.

We show that the degree of intrinsic FC within a widely distributed auditory network that includes right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), in addition to bilateral auditory cortices, is negatively correlated with regularization of melodic material during memory retrieval.

results.result: The study included 52 right-handed volunteers with normal hearing (33 females, mean age 24.5 years), of whom 51 completed the entire experiment. All participants were musically naive (mean 0.6 years ± 0.98 of formal training), and the two experimental sessions were separated by an average of 20 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 provide clear methodological details about participant characteristics and study design. The sample size (N=51 completers from 52 enrolled), demographic information, musical training exclusion criteria, and temporal separation between sessions are all explicitly stated with appropriate descriptive statistics.

results.result: The oddball task used tone sequences from the Bohlen-Pierce scale, with standard sequences (80% of trials) interspersed with contour deviants (10%) and interval deviants (10%). Contour deviants violated melodic contour but not interval size, while interval deviants violated interval size but not contour. Two deviant sequences of the same type were presented in close succession to enhance BOLD response.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C28 describe the stimulus design and experimental paradigm in detail. The use of the Bohlen-Pierce scale is documented with citation (C21), the trial proportions are explicitly stated (C23-C25), and the deviant types are clearly defined (C26-C27). The methodological rationale for paired deviants is provided (C28).

results.result: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner using multiband EPI sequences. Resting-state fMRI (600 volumes over 10 min) and functional localizer data (1535 volumes over 25 min) were collected. Data were preprocessed using SPM12 and the CONN toolbox, with band-pass filtering at 0.008-0.09 Hz. Four ROIs were defined as 5 mm spheres centered on peak activations from the functional localizer.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 provide comprehensive technical details about MRI acquisition and preprocessing. Scanner specifications, sequence parameters (TR, TE, voxel size), volume counts, software versions (SPM12 r7487, Matlab R2016b), and preprocessing steps including filtering parameters are all explicitly documented. ROI definition methodology is clearly described.

results.result: Signaling games involved sender-receiver pairs exchanging melodic signals (five-tone sequences from the BP scale) associated with five emotions (facial expressions). Each participant played 70 trials in Game 1 (as receiver) and 30 trials in Game 2 (as sender). By design, confederate senders never adjusted their code in Game 1, resulting in asymmetry of -1.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe the signaling game paradigm with appropriate citations to Lewis (1969) and the authors' previous work. The stimuli (melodic patterns and emotional states), trial numbers, and experimental design features (fixed roles, confederate behavior) are clearly specified. The asymmetry measure is defined and its expected value in Game 1 is stated.

results.result: In Game 2, asymmetry was significantly negative (median -0.4, Z=-6.05, p<0.001), indicating participants as senders maintained their code while receivers adjusted more. Coordination in Game 1 was significantly positive for both tone (median 0.76) and contour distance (median 0.84, Z=6.21, p<0.001). Transmission was positive and significant, with better accuracy for contour (median 0.65, Z=6.22, p<0.001) than tone distance (median 0.36, Z=6.21, p<0.001). All participants successfully learned and transmitted the initial material.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 report behavioral results with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed rank tests) and effect sizes. The asymmetry, coordination, and transmission measures are all significantly different from zero with reported medians, Z-scores, and p-values. The interpretation that contour information was transmitted more faithfully than interval information is supported by the comparative statistics.

results.result: Innovation was positive and significant for both tone and contour distance (both median 0.64, p<0.001). In Game 2, melodic signals became less entropic, especially in contour (mean change 0.07, Z=4.42, p<0.001), and were biased toward smaller intervals (mean ICR change 0.15, Z=-3.92, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 report structural changes in the transmitted material with appropriate statistics. However, C46 notes identical medians (0.64) for tone and contour innovation despite claiming one is higher than the other, which appears to be a reporting error in the manuscript. The entropy reduction (C47) and interval compression (C48) are both statistically significant with proper test statistics reported.

results.result: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant bilateral STG activations (pFWE<0.001) for contour deviants versus standards, with four distinct clusters: two anterior in Heschl's gyrus (HG) and two posterior in planum temporale (PT). No significant activations were detected for interval deviants versus standards.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 report fMRI localizer results with appropriate statistical thresholds and anatomical localization. The bilateral STG activation pattern is clearly described with reference to cytoarchitectonic areas (Te1, Te1.2, Te3) and supported by Figure 4 and Table 2. The null result for interval deviants (C51) is explicitly stated and consistent with the study's focus on contour processing.

results.result: Individuals with stronger interhemispheric rs-FC between lateral STG ROIs showed better learning performance and less innovation. Fisher's z values were positively correlated with coordination (r=0.41, p=0.002), accuracy (r=0.36, p=0.007), and transmission (r=0.41, p=0.002), and negatively correlated with innovation (r=-0.41, p=0.003). A negative correlation was also observed between innovation and rs-FC between left STG and left HG (r=-0.41, p=0.002).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 report the primary brain-behavior correlations with appropriate Bonferroni correction (α=0.05/7=0.007). All reported correlations survive correction and show moderate effect sizes (r=0.36-0.41). The pattern is internally consistent: stronger connectivity predicts better learning/transmission and less innovation. Statistical tests and effect sizes are properly reported.

results.result: Fisher's z values between left and right HG were positively correlated with regularization of melodic contour (r=0.43, p=0.001).
results.evaluation: Claim C58 reports a significant correlation between interhemispheric HG connectivity and contour regularization that survives Bonferroni correction. The effect size (r=0.43) is moderate and the statistical significance is clearly stated. This finding is distinct from the learning/transmission results and suggests a dissociation in the network.

results.result: Whole-brain analysis revealed that FC between left HG and right middle/superior frontal gyri was negatively correlated with melodic regularization (r=-0.58, p<0.001). Individuals who produced smoother melodic material in Game 2 had stronger negative correlation between left primary auditory cortex and right prefrontal regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 report a significant frontotemporal connectivity pattern predicting regularization behavior. The correlation is stronger (r=-0.58) than the ROI-to-ROI effects and survives cluster-level FWE correction (p<0.05). The interpretation (C60) follows logically from the statistical result, though the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Digit span scores did not predict learning behavior or structural regularization. Task-based activation levels (percent signal change) in the ROIs did not predict behavior or structural changes. Task-dependent functional connectivity (PPI analysis) also did not predict behavioral outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 report null results for alternative predictors. These negative findings are important controls showing specificity of the rs-FC effects. The lack of relationship with digit span (C61) suggests the effects are not due to general working memory capacity. The null results for task activation (C62) and task-dependent connectivity (C63) support the authors' interpretation that intrinsic connectivity, not task-evoked activity, drives the behavioral effects.

results.result: Rs-FC between homologous left and right STG regions predicts individual behavior in learning, transmission, and reorganization of artificial tone systems. Structural reorganization was specifically predicted by rs-FC between bilateral Heschl's gyri and between left HG and prefrontal regions, while learning and transmission were predicted by rs-FC between bilateral planum temporale. This suggests a functional dissociation in the bilateral fronto-temporal auditory network.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 synthesize the main findings into a coherent result. The dissociation between HG (regularization) and PT (learning/transmission) is supported by the pattern of correlations in C52-C60. However, the claim that learning/transmission were 'only' predicted by PT connectivity (C66) may be overstated given that C53-C55 report correlations with lateral STG (which includes both HG and PT regions). The functional dissociation interpretation (C67) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The degree of interhemispheric rs-FC within fronto-temporal auditory networks predicts—weeks after scanning—learning, transmission, and structural modification of an artificial tone system. These findings point to interhemispheric functional connectivity as a neural source of inter-individual variation in social learning, symbolic transmission, and structural modification of symbolic systems. This may be the first demonstration of specific neurophysiological mechanisms underlying perceptuo-cognitive biases in music evolution, and such variability may give rise to system-level variation in musical systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C107-C109 present the study's main conclusions. The predictive relationship between rs-FC and behavior weeks later (C3) is well-supported by the correlation results. The broader interpretation about cultural transmission (C107) is reasonable given the experimental design. The novelty claim (C108) is appropriately hedged ('may be the first'), and the speculation about population-level effects (C109) is supported by citations to relevant theoretical and empirical work, though it extends beyond the current data.

results.result: The bilateral STG activation includes main cortical generators of auditory MMN and reflects auditory change-detection and bottom-up auditory scene analysis processes. The absence of significant activations for interval deviants is consistent with previous findings that automatic detection in non-musicians is more difficult for pitch interval changes than contour changes. The results support the view that automatic detection and pre-attentive auditory scene analysis are primarily carried out in early auditory cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 interpret the fMRI localizer results in the context of established literature on MMN and auditory scene analysis. The interpretations are well-supported by multiple citations and consistent with the observed activation pattern. The explanation for the null interval deviant result (C71) is reasonable and supported by prior work on non-musicians and unfamiliar scales.

results.result: The 'neuronal recycling' hypothesis proposes that cultural systems are accommodated within pre-existing brain networks and may be shaped by their computational constraints. Auditory scene analysis emerges early in development, is automatic and conserved across species, and its neural circuitry might be evolutionarily older than human musicality, potentially providing neuronal substrates for cultural recycling of music.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 present theoretical background from the literature with appropriate citations. These are well-established ideas in cognitive neuroscience and evolutionary musicology that provide context for the study's findings. The claims are properly attributed to prior work and serve to motivate the current investigation.

results.result: A positive correlation was observed between interhemispheric rs-FC in bilateral PT and accuracy in learning and transmitting melodic material. This is consistent with prior findings that increased interhemispheric FC in STG is associated with facilitated melodic encoding and discrimination, and that increased PT connectivity is associated with superior auditory skills like absolute pitch and enhanced language-related skills in musicians. These findings support a model of PT as a computational hub for spectro-temporal analysis and suggest that spontaneous interhemispheric correlation patterns may reflect prior constraints on auditory learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 contextualize the current findings within established literature on interhemispheric auditory connectivity. The citations to prior work on TMS effects (C79), absolute pitch (C81), and musician advantages (C82) are appropriate and support the interpretation. The theoretical synthesis (C83-C84) is reasonable though somewhat speculative, particularly regarding the mechanistic interpretation of rs-FC patterns.

results.result: Two mechanisms may account for the rs-FC effects: (1) coherence of spontaneous fluctuations may reflect synaptic efficacy structure that modulates information exchange efficiency during learning, and (2) interindividual variability in structural connectivity between bilateral homologous auditory regions (partly mediated by corpus callosum) is strongly associated with FC. Interhemispheric rs-FC between homologous areas is a functional organization principle of the human brain, and more efficient interhemispheric communication may account for enhanced learning and transmission performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 propose mechanistic explanations for the observed rs-FC effects. While both mechanisms are plausible and supported by citations to relevant literature, they remain speculative in the context of this study. The authors did not measure structural connectivity or synaptic properties directly, so these interpretations, while reasonable, go beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The claims are appropriately hedged with 'may' and 'might.'

results.result: No evidence was found for a relationship between behavioral performance and task-related brain activations, suggesting that intrinsic connectivity properties of the auditory network, rather than activation levels, drive social learning and structural modification. This is consistent with previous ERP findings that only MMN latencies (not amplitudes) predicted behavior. ERP latencies may reflect axonal myelination and diffusion properties determining FC, while amplitudes relate to population size. This supports the view that spontaneous neuronal synchronization is a more efficient metric of neural information processing than task-related activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 interpret the null results for task activation and connect them to prior ERP findings. The consistency with previous work (C91) strengthens the interpretation. The proposed distinction between latency (connectivity-related) and amplitude (population size) effects (C92-C93) is supported by appropriate citations. However, the broader claim about spontaneous synchronization being 'more efficient' (C94) is somewhat speculative and may overinterpret the null results.

results.result: During cultural transmission, information may become increasingly compressible and structured. Early auditory regions (HG and PT) are critical for encoding and retention of melodic information. The degree of intrinsic FC within a distributed auditory network including right DLPFC and bilateral auditory cortices is negatively correlated with regularization of melodic material during memory retrieval. Individuals with stronger negative correlation (antiphase coherence) between DLPFC and auditory cortices introduce smoother melodic forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 present the regularization findings and their theoretical context. The negative correlation between DLPFC-auditory connectivity and regularization (C97-C98) is well-supported by the statistical results (C59). The background on compressibility (C95) and auditory encoding (C96) is appropriately cited. This represents a novel and unexpected finding that extends beyond the initial hypotheses.

results.result: DLPFC supports maintenance, monitoring, and manipulation of perceptual representations in posterior sensory regions. Reduced DLPFC-sensory connectivity may affect mnemonic information quality, resulting in loss of details and emphasis on global features. In amusics, reduced frontotemporal connectivity and overconnected auditory cortices are linked to impaired melodic retrieval. This pattern suggests that increased bilateral auditory connectivity with decreased frontotemporal connectivity reveals poorer auditory processing and may explain regularization in cultural material acquisition.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 propose a mechanistic interpretation of the DLPFC findings by analogy to congenital amusia. While the parallel is interesting and the amusia literature is appropriately cited (C101-C102), the interpretation is speculative. The current study found that individuals with stronger negative DLPFC-auditory correlation regularized more, but this pattern is not directly equivalent to the reduced connectivity seen in amusics. The mechanistic explanation (C100) is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Small differences in the functional architecture at rest of temporo-frontal networks can manifest in regularization behaviors in a single round of learning and transmission. These differences can be amplified by cultural transmission to produce population-level effects, as shown by computational, behavioral, and population-genetics studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by the current data showing individual differences in rs-FC predict regularization behavior. However, C106's claim about amplification to population-level effects is speculative and extends beyond the current study's single-generation design. While the authors cite relevant theoretical and empirical work, the current study does not directly demonstrate amplification across multiple transmission events or population-level effects.

results.result: Music producers vary in their ability to acquire and transmit music, which may serve as a mechanism for emergence of new musical traits. Symbolic systems evolve during transmission, partly adapting to brain properties. Laboratory experiments show artificial signaling systems become organized during transmission. Musical traits may be traced to auditory cortex functioning, with music material passing through an information processing bottleneck instantiated in connectivity patterns. Functional connectivity is associated with melodic encoding and discrimination, and rs-FC networks may indicate auditory learning skills. Previous work showed MMN latency predicts learning and transmission in signaling games, suggesting cultural transmission may be constrained by auditory cortex organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 provide theoretical and empirical background for the study, drawing on cultural evolution theory, neuroscience of music perception, and the authors' previous work. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. This background establishes the rationale for investigating rs-FC as a predictor of cultural transmission behaviors and connects the current work to broader questions in music evolution and cultural transmission.

results.result: Rs-FC measures temporal correlation of spontaneous slow fluctuations (<0.1 Hz) in BOLD signal between spatially separated brain regions. It captures spontaneous interactions between neuronal populations in functionally associated networks and is recognized as a promising tool for assessing individual differences in brain function.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 define the rs-FC measure used in the study with appropriate citations to foundational work (Biswal, 2012; Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Dubois and Adolphs, 2016). This methodological background is accurate and establishes the rationale for using rs-FC to study individual differences.

results.result: Task-driven activations did not predict behavior in signaling games.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 summarizes the null results for task-based activation reported in C62. This is an important negative finding that supports the specificity of the rs-FC effects and is appropriately reported.
